Crucially, we replicated the main results from our prior studies: Participants were significantly more likely to sacrifice a future salary increase if it could help them avoid getting a bad leader (48.1%) than to obtain a good leader (37.7%), reflecting an average choice difference of 10.4 percentage points, OR = 1.60, 95% CI [1.47, 1.75], p < .001.

table.text: As part of a problem-solving study, all participants were informed at the beginning of the session that ten participants would be randomly selected to receive their assigned supervisor for a follow-up task worth up to £10, and to complete the actual work task in question.

In a between-subjects design, participants were asked to make a choice of whether they would sacrifice some of their earnings either to obtain the good leader rather than getting the average leader, or to avoid the bad leader rather than getting the average leader, depending on condition.

Once again, the results provided clear support for our bad-leader aversion hypothesis: Participants were significantly more likely to sacrifice real money to avoid getting a bad leader (54.5%) than to obtain a good leader (43.3%) in a future work task, OR = 1.57, 95% CI [1.23, 2.00], p < .001 (see Figure 4), reflecting an average choice difference of 11.2 percentage points.

table.header: Study 4: Replication in Norwegian Student Sample

table.text: As secondary outcome measures, participants were asked about the perceived impact of the new leader on their future happiness at work, work motivation, job task completion, and organizational trust.

As the main outcome measures, participants were asked if they would be willing to spend an hour of their free time to vote and if they would sacrifice a 5% salary increase, framed identically to Study 3.
We recruited 1,955 participants (Mage = 42.05, SD = 14.00; 49.1% female) from the United States via Prolific.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 (valence: Good vs. bad) × 2 (domain: Morality vs. competence) between-subjects design.
As secondary outcome measures, participants were asked how they would feel if their organization hired the leader and how much they would trust their employer.

As the main outcome measures, participants were asked if they would be willing to spend an hour of their free time to vote and if they would sacrifice a 5% salary increase, framed identically to the previous experiments.
We recruited 47,719 participants (Mage = 42.83, SD = 15.25; 51.6% female), roughly 1,000 each from 40 countries, using a global data collection agency.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: Moral leader, immoral leader, competent leader, or incompetent leader.

As exploratory measures, participants were first asked how they would feel if their organization hired the leader, where they chose between "less happy at work than before", "no difference", and "more happy at work than before", and how much they would trust their employer, where they chose between "less than before", "no difference", and "more than before".

Importantly, as the main outcome measure, participants were asked if they would be willing to sacrifice a 5% increase in their salary if it could guarantee that the good leader is hired (moral and competent conditions), or if it could guarantee that the bad leader is not hired (immoral and incompetent conditions).

To test our pre-registered hypotheses, we estimated a series of multilevel binary logistic regressions with salary sacrifice (0 = No,1 = Yes) as the outcome Participants were instructed to answer all subsequent questions as though they had been selected, because there was a real chance they would be.
Participants were then informed that if selected, they would be assigned one of two pre-evaluated supervisors.
In both conditions, participants were told the supervisor would be randomly selected between Supervisor A and Supervisor B with an equal 50-50 probability unless they chose to intervene.
As the main outcome measure, participants were asked whether they would sacrifice £1 from their £5 future base payment to influence their supervisor assignment.
We received complete responses from 1,099 US-based participants recruited using Prolific.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Good leader condition or bad leader condition.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: The aversive effect of bad leaders - A Norwegian student sample
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The main question in this study is whether people are more strongly motivated to avoid bad leaders than they are to get good leaders.

The two primary hypotheses in the experiment are the following:
H1: Participants will be more likely to make an effort to vote in an organizational election to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
H2: Participants will be more likely to give up a 5% pay raise to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
table.design_dependent_variables:
As dependent variables (outcome measures), the participants will make two binary choices (yes/no) based on a hypothetical workplace scenario.

The starting point in the scenario is that the participant works in an organization that has a neutral or "average" leader, in which the board is planning to hire a long-term replacement. The participant learns from a friend that the candidate for getting the job is either a very good leader OR a very bad leader (in terms of competence and morality), depending on condition (good vs. bad).

After reading this scenario, where the only difference between the two conditions is whether the new leader candidate is described as good or bad, the participants will make a series of judgments about the perceived impact of the new leader (on their own happiness, work motivation, job task completion, and organizational trust), as potential mediator variables, before they will make two hypothetical choices as the two primary outcome measures:

DV1: Whether they would make an effort to vote in an internal election, for or against this new leader candidate (yes/no).
DV2: Whether they would be willing to give up a 5% salary increase to make sure that the new leader would get hired or not (yes/no).
table.study_design_overview: Two conditions: Hypothetical choices EITHER concerning a bad future leader OR a good future leader, between-subjects.
table.statistical_tests:
H1: To test the prediction that participants in the 'Bad Leader' condition will be more likely to choose to participate in an organizational election than participants in the 'Good Leader' condition, I will conduct a chi-square test (p<.05, two-tailed).

H2: To test the prediction that participants in the 'Bad Leader' condition will be more likely to sacrifice a future pay increase to avoid getting a bad leader than participants in the 'Good Leader' condition will be to secure a good leader, I will conduct a second chi-square test (p<.05, two-tailed).
table.outliers_and_exclusions: I will include all participants who pass a simple attention check at the beginning ("Please respond with the number 0 to the question below") and then complete the full survey.
table.sample_size: I will recruit Norwegian student participants via e-mail invitations from the 25th of February to the 1st of April (2022), with a goal of recruiting a minimum of 350 participants. The response rate is difficult to predict, and so is the final sample size. As long as I pass 350 students by the 1st of April, I will not collect more data for this experiment after that date.
table.additional_comments:
As a test of potential explanatory mechanisms, I will conduct a mediation analysis including the four judgment variables (perceived impact of the new leader on their future happiness at work, work motivation, job task completion, and organizational trust), to examine whether a similar negative dominance effect on any of these variables will mediate the stronger effect of bad (vs. good) leaders on each of the two choice outcomes.

As background measures, I will record age, gender, education, number of years in the workforce, previous experience with leaders (0=Very bad, 5=Neutral, 10=Very good), and political orientation.

table.title: Good vs. Bad Leaders: Competence and Morality
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching question is whether people are more motivated to avoid bad leaders than they are to get good leaders. Participants will read a workplace scenario focusing either on a good or bad leader, based either on the general competence or the general morality of this leader (2x2). The four primary hypotheses in this experiment are the following:

H1a: When competence is the focal person characteristic, participants will be more likely to make an effort to vote in an organizational election to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
H1b: When competence is the focal person characteristic, participants will be more likely to give up a 5% pay raise to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
H2a: When morality is the focal person characteristic, participants will be more likely to make an effort to vote in an organizational election to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
H2b: When morality is the focal person characteristic, participants will be more likely to give up a 5% pay raise to avoid getting a bad leader than to get a good leader.
table.design_dependent_variables:
As dependent variables (outcome measures), participants will make two binary choices (yes/no) based on the hypothetical workplace scenario. The starting point in the scenario is that the participant works in an organization that has a neutral or "average" leader, in which the board is planning to hire a long-term replacement. The participant learns from a friend that the candidate for getting the job is either a very good leader (top 20%) OR a very bad leader (bottom 20%), either in terms of their competence OR morality, depending on condition (2x2).

After reading this scenario, all participants will make a series of judgments about the perceived impact of the new leader (on their happiness, work motivation, job task performance, and organizational trust) as potential mediator variables, before they will make two hypothetical choices as the two primary outcome measures:

DV1: Whether they would make an effort to vote in an internal election, for or against this new leader candidate (yes/no).
DV2: Whether they would be willing to give up a 5% salary increase to make sure that the new leader would get hired or not (yes/no).
table.study_design_overview: Four conditions. Participants will make hypothetical choices concerning either a bad OR good potential leader, based on a description of either their competence OR morality, between-subjects (2x2 design).
table.statistical_tests: I will conduct a separate chi-square test (p<.05, two-tailed) for each of the 4 primary hypotheses (H1a, H1b, H2a, H2b), to test the prediction that participants will be more likely to actively engage to avoid a bad leader than getting a good leader both in the dimension of competence (H1a and H1b) and morality (H2a and H2b).

table.title: Bad Leader 40 Country May 2025
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching research question is whether people have a stronger motivation to avoid a bad leader than to get a good leader. Bad leaders are operationalized as immoral (morality domain) or incompetent (competence domain). Good leaders are operationalized as moral (morality domain) or competent (competence domain).

We will test the following hypotheses:
H1. People are more likely to sacrifice a 5% increase in salary to avoid a bad (immoral or incompetent) leader than to get a good (moral or competent) leader. 
H2a. People are more likely to sacrifice a 5% increase in salary to avoid an immoral leader than to get a moral leader. 
H2b. People are more likely to sacrifice a 5% increase in salary to avoid an incompetent leader than to get a competent leader.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Our main dependent variable is whether participants will choose to sacrifice a 5% salary increase or not (binary choice), in a hypothetical workplace scenario. 
In the two bad leader conditions (immoral or incompetent), participants will be asked: Would you be willing to sacrifice a 5% increase of your salary, if it could guarantee that your organization would NOT hire such a bad leader as your closest supervisor?
In the two good leader conditions (moral or competent), participants will be asked: Would you be willing to sacrifice a 5% increase of your salary, if it could guarantee that your organization would hire such a good leader as your closest supervisor?
In all four conditions, participants will be presented with two choice options: "No: I would not sacrifice my salary increase", and "Yes: I would sacrifice my salary increase".
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 (leader: bad vs. good) × 2 (domain: morality vs. competence) between-subjects experiment design. 

Participants will be asked to imagine a scenario where their employer plans to hire a new leader, in which the previous leader is considered rather neutral or average. In the bad leader conditions, the new leader candidate will be described as being in the bottom 20% of leaders working in similar organizations, either in terms of their moral character or competence. In the good leader conditions, the leader will be described as being in the top 20% of leaders working in similar organizations, either in terms of their moral character or competence.
table.statistical_tests:
To test the simple main effects predicted by H1, H2a, and H2b, we will estimate a series of multi-level binary logistic regressions with salary sacrifice decision (0 = No, 1 = Yes) as the outcome, random intercepts for countries, and random slopes for the leader condition across countries. If a random slopes model fails to converge, we will include only random intercepts for countries. If the random intercepts model still fails to converge, we will use a fixed-effects logistic regression (no random effects) with country included as a fixed-effect control variable.

We will use an alpha level of 5% for all estimated coefficients and pairwise comparisons, in which an effect in the predicted direction at p < .05 (two-tailed) will be interpreted as support for the hypothesis. 
For each model, leader condition (good = 0, bad = 1) will be the predictor. For testing H1, we will use the full dataset. For testing H2a, we will use data only from the two morality conditions. For testing H2b, we will use data only from the two competence conditions. 

For each model, in the case of model convergence with random effects and intercepts, we estimate random effects with 95% CIs to obtain information about between-country variation and visualize these.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded if they fail an attention check at the beginning of the study. When testing each of the hypotheses, all other participants who have completed the respective variable measures will be included.
table.sample_size: This study has a predetermined sample size of 40,000 participants (40 countries; 1,000 participants per country), as it is part of a larger data collection.
table.additional_comments:
Secondary analyses:
To explore potential mediation of the simple main effects hypothesized in H1, H2a, and H2b, we will collect two measures: happiness at work and organizational trust. 
Participants will be asked, "If the board should decide to hire this new leader, how would you feel about it?", where they will report their expected feelings (less happy at work than before/no difference/more happy at work than before) and trust in their employer (less than before/no difference/more than before). For the bad leader conditions, less happy/trust will be coded as 1, and the other two options as 0. For the good leader conditions, more happy/trust will be coded as 1 and the other two options as 0. 
To test for potential mediation, we will estimate three multi-level structural equation models (one each for H1, H2a, and H2b) with clustered errors at the country-level and the two mediators added in parallel to explain the effect of bad versus good leader on the salary-sacrifice decision. We generally expect the proportion of participants expecting less happiness/less trust in the bad conditions to be higher than the proportion expecting more happiness/more trust in the good conditions, which in turn might be associated with a higher likelihood of salary-sacrifice choice in the bad leader conditions. 

To explore potential moderation of the simple main effects predicted in H1, H2a, and H2b by political orientation, we will re-estimate the model from #5, adding a multiplicative interaction between leader condition and political orientation of participants (single item, scale: 1 = Far left, 4 = Center, 7 = Far right). We expect the bad vs. good effect to be stronger for participants on the left than on the right.

Exploratory analyses: 
To compare good versus bad leader effects across morality and competence domains, we will estimate a secondary multi-level binary logistic regression model with salary-sacrifice decision (0 = No, 1 = Yes) as the outcome, random intercepts for countries, and fixed effects predictors of leader (0 = good, 1 = bad), domain (0 = competence, 1 = morality), and their interaction. We will use the same model convergence alternatives as specified in #5.

table.title: Bad Leader Incentive Study April 2026
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching research question is whether people have a stronger motivation to avoid a bad leader than to get a good leader, when measured with a real incentivized choice concerning a future supervised task. 

In this study, bad leaders are operationalized as very immoral and incompetent (scoring very low on both moral character and competence), and good leaders are operationalized as very moral and competent (scoring very high on both moral character and competence).

Participants will first complete a number series reasoning task and be told that 10 participants will be randomly selected and invited to participate in a 30-minute group problem-solving study the following week, where they will work with a supervisor and can choose to sacrifice £1 from their £5 future-study base payment to influence which supervisor they are assigned.

We will test the following hypothesis:
H1: People are more likely to sacrifice real money to avoid a bad leader (immoral and incompetent) than to get a good leader (moral and competent).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Our main dependent variable is whether participants will choose to sacrifice £1 from their £5 future-study base payment (binary choice), in an incentive-compatible task context. In the bad leader condition, participants will be asked: Do you want to sacrifice £1 from your future base payment, reducing it from £5 to £4, to guarantee that you will NOT get Supervisor B (a very immoral and incompetent person), and instead will get Supervisor A (average moral character and competence)? 

In the good leader condition, participants will be asked: Do you want to sacrifice £1 from your future base payment, reducing it from £5 to £4, to guarantee that you will get Supervisor B (a very moral and competent person), rather than Supervisor A (average moral character and competence)? In both conditions, if participants choose not to sacrifice, their supervisor will remain a random 50-50 draw between Supervisor A and Supervisor B.

Within each condition, the framing of the choice option alternatives will also be randomly varied between-subjects, while keeping the substantial content of the choice the same. Specifically, in the bad leader condition, one version presents the DV choice as "Yes: I choose to sacrifice £1 to avoid Supervisor B (getting Supervisor A)" and the other as "Yes: I choose to sacrifice £1 to get Supervisor A (avoiding Supervisor B)." In the good leader condition, one version presents the choice as "Yes: I choose to sacrifice £1 to get Supervisor B (avoiding Supervisor A)" and the other as "Yes: I choose to sacrifice £1 to avoid Supervisor A (getting Supervisor B)." In both versions, the "No" option reads: "No: I choose not sacrificing £1 (random 50-50 selection proceeds between Supervisor A and B)." For our main analyses, we will collapse across the two framing versions.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions in a between-subjects design: A bad leader or good leader condition. In both conditions, Supervisor A is described as scoring 5 out of 10 on both moral character and competence (average). 

In the bad leader condition, Supervisor B is described as scoring [0 or 1] out of 10, rated very low on both moral character and competence-meaning they are generally perceived to be an immoral and incompetent person. In the good leader condition, Supervisor B is described as scoring [9 or 10] out of 10, rated very high on both moral character and competence-meaning they are generally perceived to be a moral and competent person.

Importantly, this study uses an incentive-compatible design. Participants are told that 10 participants from the study will be randomly selected for a future group study, and they must answer all questions assuming they could be selected, because there is a real chance they will be. The sacrifice of £1 would be real and consequential for selected participants.
table.statistical_tests: To test H1, we will estimate a binary logistic regression with the sacrifice decision (0 = No, 1 = Yes) as the outcome and leader condition (0 = good, 1 = bad) as the predictor. We will use an alpha level of 5%, in which an effect in the predicted direction (p < .05, two-tailed) will be interpreted as support for the hypothesis.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will include only responses from participants who fully complete the survey. From fully completed responses, we will exclude participants who:
1. Fail the visual perception bot check (selecting anything other than "Blue Line"), OR
2. Fail the Atlantic Ocean attention check (selecting "Strongly agree" or "Agree"), OR
3. Fail all comprehension check questions.
table.sample_size: We plan to recruit 1,100 participants via Prolific before any exclusions. We will stop data collection when Prolific notifies that 1,100 complete responses have been received.
table.additional_comments:
To explore potential mediation of the main effect predicted by H1, we will collect three mediator measures. After the sacrifice choice, participants will be asked: "If you were to learn that Supervisor B (rather than Supervisor A) has been assigned to you, how do you think this would affect your…" (a) happiness and well-being during the task (1 = Much less happy, 5 = Much more happy), (b) trust in the leader during the task (1 = Much less trust, 5 = Much more trust), and (c) performance during the task (1 = Much worse performance, 5 = Much better performance).

As exploratory analysis, we might estimate a mediation model (bootstrapped indirect effects), 10,000 resamples) with the three mediators added in parallel to explain the effect of bad versus good leader on the monetary sacrifice decision. We generally expect that participants in the bad leader condition will anticipate lower happiness, trust, and performance when assigned Supervisor B compared to participants in the good leader condition, which in turn might be associated with a higher likelihood of making the monetary sacrifice choice in the bad leader condition.

We will also collect the following background and demographic information: Age, gender, education level, income, and political orientation.

live_data_statements: Study 3 (N = 385 US-based Prolific participants; Mage = 35.25, SD = 13.58; 47.0% female) provides the first causal test of whether people are more motivated to avoid the worst leaders than to obtain the best ones.

Consistent with our primary hypothesis, participants were more likely to vote in an internal election to avoid a bad leader (84.9%) than to obtain a good leader (66.8%), OR = 2.79, 95% CI [1.71, 4.63], p < .001, and they were also more likely to give up a future salary increase to avoid a bad leader (46.9%) than to obtain a good leader (24.4%), OR = 2.74, 95% CI [1.78, 4.25], p < .001.

Study 5 (N = 1,955 US-based Prolific participants; Mage = 42.05, SD = 14.00; 49.1% female) examined whether the aversion to bad leaders operates similarly across the two person-perception dimensions of moral character and competence, using a factorial 2 (valence: Good vs. bad) x 2 (dimension: Competence vs. morality) between-subjects design.

Within the morality domain, participants were more likely to vote to avoid an immoral leader (82.9%) than to obtain a moral leader (75.1%), OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.18, 2.20], p = .003, and more likely to sacrifice a future salary increase to avoid an immoral leader (50.5%) than to obtain a moral leader (28.6%), OR = 2.55, 95% CI [1.96, 3.33], p < .001.

Within the competence domain as well, participants were more likely to vote to avoid an incompetent leader (79.5%) than to obtain a competent leader (63.4%), OR = 2.24, 95% CI [1.69, 2.99], p < .001, and to sacrifice a future salary increase to avoid an incompetent leader (30.1%) than to obtain a competent leader (15.6%), OR = 2.33, 95% CI [1.71, 3.19], p < .001.
Across all conditions in this global sample, 42.9% of participants were willing to sacrifice a 5% salary increase to influence the leader assignment in a workplace context.

Crucially, we replicated the main results from our prior studies: Participants were significantly more likely to sacrifice a future salary increase if it could help them avoid getting a bad leader (48.1%) than to obtain a good leader (37.7%), reflecting an average choice difference of 10.4 percentage points, OR = 1.60, 95% CI [1.47, 1.75], p < .001.

As part of a problem-solving study, all participants were informed at the beginning of the session that ten participants would be randomly selected to receive their assigned supervisor for a follow-up task worth up to £10, and to complete the actual work task in question.

In a between-subjects design, participants were asked to make a choice of whether they would sacrifice some of their earnings either to obtain the good leader rather than getting the average leader, or to avoid the bad leader rather than getting the average leader, depending on condition.

Once again, the results provided clear support for our bad-leader aversion hypothesis: Participants were significantly more likely to sacrifice real money to avoid getting a bad leader (54.5%) than to obtain a good leader (43.3%) in a future work task, OR = 1.57, 95% CI [1.23, 2.00], p < .001 (see Figure 4), reflecting an average choice difference of 11.2 percentage points.

text.text: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1 , and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership [2] [3] [4] .
text.formatted: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1 , and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> .

text.text: Yet, according to Popper 5 , the central question of institutional design is not who should rule, but how to prevent bad leaders from doing too much damage.
This raises the question of which approach is more consistent with human psychology: Aim for the best leaders, or avoid the worst?
We provide robust evidence for an "avoid-the-worst" principle in human leadership preferences.

Although text analyses indicated that the top 100 business schools emphasize good leadership far more than the prevention of bad leadership, actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews show that people mentioned their leader 70% more often in the negative than positive section, and negative leader mentions predicted company ratings 1.5 times more strongly.

Providing causal evidence, five high-powered experiments across 40 countries (N = 51,433) revealed that people were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than obtaining a good leader-across morality and competence, hypothetical and incentivized choice, ideology and culture.
People care more about avoiding the worst leaders than getting the best.
Society invests heavily in developing and selecting the best leaders.

For instance, global estimates suggest that organizations spend over $60 billion per year on leadership training 1 , which is more than the total UN spending per year on global development and humanitarian activities combined 6 .
What do they learn?

As the academic starting point, the field of leadership research shows clear signs of "excessive positivity" 2 , by focusing on the constructive and so-called transformational potential of leaders far more than the destructive and harmful potential 3, 7 .
text.formatted: As the academic starting point, the field of leadership research shows clear signs of "excessive positivity" 2 , by focusing on the constructive and so-called transformational potential of leaders far more than the destructive and harmful potential <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, a meta-analysis of over 1200 leadership studies on job engagement and burnout found that 74% focused on constructive leadership whereas only 15% focused on destructive leadership 4 .
In the popularized management literature as well, a common focus has been how leaders can go "from good to great" 8 .

In contrast with this positive leaning in current leadership research, Karl Popper 5 argued in his political philosophy that the central question of institutional design is not "who should rule?", as posed by Plato, but rather: How can we prevent bad or incompetent leaders from doing too much damage?
In Popper's view, the chief role of citizens and institutions is not to select the best leader, but to block or remove bad ones from power through peaceful means.
This view suggests that institutions should aim to minimize tyranny from the worst leaders, rather than to maximize the gains from the best ones.
Building on Popper's theory, originally focusing on political institutions and democracy, we extend it and make the same logic empirically testable in an organizational context.
These conflicting perspectives raise a fundamental question: Which approach is more consistent with human psychology?

Across the world, do people lean in the positive direction by focusing mostly on obtaining the best leaders, or do they support a Popperian precautionary logic by prioritizing protection against the worst ones?

We operationalize the "best" and "worst" leaders as those at the extreme ends of leadership quality (e.g., top or bottom 20%), across two broad perception dimensions that are fundamental for how people see and evaluate each other in social life: Competence and morality [9] [10] [11] [12] , sometimes described as competence and warmth, which also applies to how leaders are perceived and evaluated 13, 14 .

text.text: The competence dimension refers to individual traits such as being knowledgeable, efficient, and intelligent, and the morality dimension refers to individual traits such as being honest, fair, and trustworthy.
Getting the best possible leader and avoiding the worst possible leader are two important goals in organizations and society.
In the current research, we explore which of these goals people are more willing to incur personal costs to achieve.

While previous research has examined the associations of good leadership [15] [16] [17] [18] and bad leadership 7, 15, 19, 20 with outcomes such as job satisfaction and performance, that evidence is primarily correlational, and does not directly compare people's motivation to obtain good leaders versus avoid bad ones.

text.text: Across seven studies, we examine the core motivation to avoid the worst leaders versus getting the best leaders in the first place, and provide both observational and causal evidence.

Study 1 uses text analysis of vision, mission, and core values statements from the world's top 100 business schools, to explore the relative priority of developing good leadership versus preventing bad leadership in current education programs.
Study 2 examines actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews from approximately 35,500 firms, to explore how people rate and react to good and bad leaders in their work life.

Five experiments (four pre-registered) then test whether people are more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than to obtain a good one, including American (Study 3) and Norwegian (Study 4) samples, separating variations in leader competence from moral character (Study 5), replicating the causal main effect across 40 countries in a cross-cultural study with broadly nationally representative samples (Study 6, N = 47,719), and finally with real monetary stakes in an incentivized choice design (Study 7).
Inspired by Popper's philosophical theory of institutional design 5 , our overarching hypothesis is that people are more motivated to avoid the worst leaders than to obtain the best leaders.

text.text: Our hypothesis is also informed by the evolutionary perspective of error management.

This theory suggests that when judgments are made under uncertainty and the costs of different errors are asymmetric, an adaptive cognitive system should be biased toward making the less costly mistake 25 .

text.text: For instance, research on the "auditory looming bias" 26 has found that people perceive approaching sounds as closer and arriving sooner than they actually do, which is consistent with the idea that overestimating the distance to an approaching threat is a costlier mistake than underestimating it.

text.text: Similarly, failing to reject a genuinely bad leader risks severe and sustained harm to oneself and the group, whereas mistakenly rejecting a genuinely good leader merely represents a lost opportunity for improvement rather than an existential threat.
There is suggestive evidence also from applied research consistent with our general hypothesis of bad-leader aversion in choice preferences.

Negative information about job candidates shapes rejection decisions more than positive information shapes acceptance decisions 27 , and negative interactions with supervisors have stronger effects on employee outcomes than positive interactions 28 .

text.text: In sum, there are psychological, evolutionary, and organizational bases for what we refer to as the "avoid-the-worst" principle in human leadership preferences: People might be more motivated to avoid the worst leaders than to obtain the best ones.
While we predict a dominant motivation to avoid bad leaders in both person perception domains, we expect the good-bad asymmetry to be stronger for morality than competence.

Whereas competence signals a person's ability to solve problems and get things done, morality signals whether the person's intentions and goals are well-meaning and socially beneficial in the first place: Will this person help or harm me?
Indeed, an immoral leader signals potential abuse, exploitation, and disregard for followers' interests, directly threatening interpersonal trust and cooperation 31, 32 .

text.text: In the current research, we will therefore study choice preferences for good versus bad leaders in general, combining morality and competence information in the same general direction, and then specifically by varying the quality of only one of these dimensions at a time.

We will now present a series of large-scale studies using different methods and participant samples, exploring the role of good versus bad leaders in people's choice preferences, along with the impact of such leaders.

Whereas Study 1 will explore the relative emphasis on developing good leadership versus preventing bad leadership in current business school education programs, Study 2 will explore the relative importance of good versus bad leaders in actual work life, based on how thousands of employees rate their organizational leadership.
Studies 3-7 will then provide a causal test of our "avoid-the-worst" principle in leadership selection, in a series of five high-powered experiments across the world.

Study 1 explored whether the official statements of the top 100 business schools per the annual Financial Times global ranking (analytic sample = 219 statements) emphasize promoting good leadership or preventing bad leadership.
We analyzed a publicly available dataset from Mendeley Data 39 .

text.text: These schools teach management and leadership skills on a considerable scale: Publicly verifiable, recent school-level figures for 47 schools alone total more than 250,000 currently enrolled students.
The official statements were coded with established promotion-focus and preventionfocus dictionaries 40 .

text.text: Promotion focus emphasizes gains and advancement, whereas prevention focus emphasizes avoiding losses and maintaining safety and security 40 , making them useful proxies for pursuing good versus avoiding bad leadership outcomes.

text.text: As a robustness test, we repeated the analyses using author-made dictionaries to compare the prevalence of aspirational-promotive language with that of precautionary-preventive language.
Results.

Top business schools used positive "promotion-focused" language (e.g., "achieve", "grow", "improve") roughly seven times more often than negative "preventionfocused" language (e.g., "avoid", "prevent", "protect") in vision statements and 2.6 times more often in mission statements.

text.text: In sum, these findings suggest that the world's top leadership education programs have a strong positive leaning.
Despite the real-life dangers of bad leadership in organizations and society, precautionary and prevention-focused content receives modest coverage.
We will now turn to the relative frequency and importance of good versus bad leadership in the workplace, when organizational leaders are judged by thousands of employees actually working for them.
Study 2 examined how employees attend to good and bad aspects of their leaders.
The leader-flagged sample contained 422,956 reviews from 4,885 firms, and the retained firms contributed 9,050,887 reviews.
We analyzed an openly available dataset of Glassdoor reviews 41 written by real employees describing their actual managers.

text.text: Glassdoor is the world's largest employee review database.

Because reviewers use separate open-ended text fields to write positive and negative aspects of their job, we can compare how often employees mention their leader when writing about pros versus cons and use those mentions to predict their overall rating of the workplace.
Study 1 found that current leadership education focuses extensively on the positive aspects of good leaders.

But if bad leaders are more psychologically impactful in real life, as our primary hypothesis predicts, then employees should mention their leader more often when describing negative aspects of their job than positive ones.

Consistent with this prediction, 65.6% of leader-flagged reviews mentioned a leader in the negative "cons" field describing their job compared to 38.4% in the positive "pros" field, which is 1.7 times as often, reflecting a 27.2 percentage-point difference (McNemar χ²(1) = 32,662, p < .001).

text.text: Leader mentions predicting outcomes.

To examine predictive validity, we tested whether leader mentions predicted overall company rating (1-5) and company recommendation to others (1 = positive,0 = negative), using reviews with non-missing outcomes from the retained firms and controlling for the length of each field outside leadermentioning chunks.

text.text: The observational findings in Studies 1 and 2 suggest that in contrast with current leadership education programs, employees seem more concerned with the prevention of bad leaders and their overall negative impact than they were with the promotion of good leaders and their overall positive impact.
However, these initial studies were purely observational.
Building on these correlational findings, Studies 3-7 will provide causal evidence from a series of controlled experiments on leadership choice preferences.

Study 3 (N = 385 US-based Prolific participants; Mage = 35.25, SD = 13.58; 47.0% female) provides the first causal test of whether people are more motivated to avoid the worst leaders than to obtain the best ones.
In a scenario-based choice experiment, the incoming candidate was said to replace the participants' current, average supervisor.

The incoming leader candidate was then described as either highly moral and competent (having very high standards across both dimensions), or immoral and incompetent (having very low standards across both dimensions).

Participants then made two binary choices: Whether they would spend their free time to vote in an internal election including the new leader, and whether they would sacrifice a salary increase in exchange for getting/not getting the leader in question.

Consistent with our primary hypothesis, participants were more likely to vote in an internal election to avoid a bad leader (84.9%) than to obtain a good leader (66.8%), OR = 2.79, 95% CI [1.71, 4.63], p < .001, and they were also more likely to give up a future salary increase to avoid a bad leader (46.9%) than to obtain a good leader (24.4%), OR = 2.74, 95% CI [1.78, 4.25], p < .001.

text.text: As in Study 3, participants read a description of an incoming leader portrayed as either very good (i.e., highly moral and competent) or very bad (i.e., highly immoral and incompetent).
Results.
Norwegian students showed the same pattern of leadership preferences as the American general population sample.

Consistent with our hypothesis, they were more likely to choose to vote in an internal election if it could help them avoid a bad leader (90.6%) rather than obtain a good leader (74.2%), OR = 3.33, 95% CI [1.80, 6.48], p < .001, and they were also more likely to choose sacrificing a future salary increase to avoid a bad leader (63.5%) than to obtain a good leader (40.5%), OR = 2.56, 95% CI [1.64, 4.03], p < .001.

text.text: Thus, Studies 3 and 4 provide causal evidence for a general aversion to bad leaders over the attraction of good leaders, in which the competence and morality dimensions of the leader were combined and varied at the same time (high competence and morality vs. low competence and morality).

Study 5 (N = 1,955 US-based Prolific participants; Mage = 42.05, SD = 14.00; 49.1% female) examined whether the aversion to bad leaders operates similarly across the two person-perception dimensions of moral character and competence, using a factorial 2 (valence: Good vs. bad) x 2 (dimension: Competence vs. morality) between-subjects design.

To further specify what a "very good" or "very bad" leader meant and ensure a symmetric experimental manipulation, the incoming leader was described as either ranking in the top or bottom 20% of leaders, on either moral character or competence.
Our primary hypothesis of bad-leader aversion was supported across both person perception domains.

Within the morality domain, participants were more likely to vote to avoid an immoral leader (82.9%) than to obtain a moral leader (75.1%), OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.18, 2.20], p = .003, and more likely to sacrifice a future salary increase to avoid an immoral leader (50.5%) than to obtain a moral leader (28.6%), OR = 2.55, 95% CI [1.96, 3.33], p < .001.

Thus, bad-leader aversion was present in both domains, but its magnitude did not differ significantly between morality and competence in the current sample.

In Study 6, we tested whether the aversion to bad leaders over the attraction of good leaders generalizes across differences in culture, institutions, and language using nationally representative samples from 40 countries covering all world regions (N = 47,719; Mage = 42.83, SD = 15.25; 51.6% female), based on age, gender, and geographic distribution.
As in Study 5, the leader was placed in either the top or bottom 20% of leaders on either moral character or general competence.
Unlike previous studies, salary sacrifice was the only included choice outcome.
Results.
Across all conditions in this global sample, 42.9% of participants were willing to sacrifice a 5% salary increase to influence the leader assignment in a workplace context.

Crucially, we replicated the main results from our prior studies: Participants were significantly more likely to sacrifice a future salary increase if it could help them avoid getting a bad leader (48.1%) than to obtain a good leader (37.7%), reflecting an average choice difference of 10.4 percentage points, OR = 1.60, 95% CI [1.47, 1.75], p < .001.

The general aversion to bad leaders was strongest in Northern, Western, and Central Europe, with Norway (OR = 2.75), France (OR = 2.62), Poland (OR = 2.44), and Finland (OR = 2.40) showing the largest asymmetries between bad versus good.

The effect was also strong in Taiwan (OR = 2.12), Italy (OR = 2.09), and South Korea (OR = 2.01), more moderate in most of the Americas and the rest of Southern Europe, and attenuated to non-significance in China and across much of Southeast Asia: China (OR = 0.98), Thailand (OR = 0.97), the Philippines (OR = 1.00), Vietnam (OR = 1.00), Indonesia (OR = 1.15), and Malaysia (OR = 1.23) all had confidence intervals crossing 1.
India was a notable case where the overall effect was significant (OR = 1.29) but driven entirely by morality (OR = 1.69), with a non-significant effect in the competence domain (OR = 1.00).

Across seven studies, we found robust evidence of aversion to bad leaders.

While leadership education at the world's top 100 business schools emphasizes promoting good leadership over preventing bad leadership in vision and mission statements (Study 1), an analysis of over 9 million job reviews from 4,885 firms finds that employees writing about their own workplaces show the opposite pattern (Study 2): People wrote more often about their bad than good leaders, and mentioning a bad leader was more predictive of the overall company rating and recommendation to others than mentioning a good leader.

We also found causal evidence of bad-leader aversion across five high-powered experiments: People were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than to obtain a good one, an asymmetry that replicated in US and Norwegian samples (Studies 3-4), held across variation in both leader morality and competence domains (Study 5), although it was stronger for morality (Study 6), generalized across 31 out of 40 countries with large differences in language, culture, and institutions (Study 6), and held with real monetary stakes (Study 7).

The aversion to bad leaders was a consistent effect that generalized around the world: Across experiments, people were 10 to 23 percentage points more likely to sacrifice time or money to avoid a bad leader than to obtain a good one.

However, the bad-leader aversion was stronger in societies characterized by high (vs. low) electoral democracy, high (vs. low) cultural individualism, high (vs. low) GDP, and low (vs. high) power distance.
These countrylevel moderators suggest that bad-leader aversion might be the strongest where people have both the norms and the channels to challenge authority.

Similarly, bad-leader aversion was also stronger among relatively higher-income individuals within countries, suggesting that economic resources may shape the motivation to engage against bad leaders at both the individual and societal levels.
Finally, the effect was found on both sides of the political spectrum, but was weaker among right-leaning than left-leaning participants.
These findings make at least three key contributions to advancing leadership research in psychology and social science.
First, we identify bad-leader aversion as a robust and globally generalizable feature of how ordinary people approach leadership selection.

While prior work has established that negative information dominates positive information in subjective experience and person perception 21, 23, 27 and that morality dominates competence in impression formation 12, 32, 34 , these findings have not been integrated or explored in human leadership preferences.

text.text: Second, we provide the first experimental test of Popper's precautionary theory of democratic institutions 5 , which we specify as an avoid-the-worst principle in leadership selection preferences.
A large literature asks what makes leaders good or effective [15] [16] [17] [18] , but a much smaller one examines the existence and consequences of destructive leadership 7, 20, 47, 48.

text.text: Crucially, neither stream of research compares the motivational pull of bad versus good leaders in the first place, when it comes to people's willingness to incur personal costs to influence the leader selection process.

Our main finding of bad-leader aversion aligns well with Popper's normative argument that the central function of democratic institutions should be to prevent the worst rather than select the best leaders 5 , and suggests that his precautionary view matches how everyday people actually think about leadership in the workplace, and especially among people living in well-functioning democracies rather than autocracies.

text.text: Third, when considering our observational and experimental evidence together, we identify a systematic disconnect between what educational institutions focus on and what people care most about in the workplace.
It is well established that leadership research has a clear positivity bias.

We find a similar positivity bias in business school education programs, which focus on the positive and aspirational aspects of leadership, whereas actual employees seem to prefer the opposite focus, as they are more concerned with avoiding the worst leaders.

Moreover, as fully reported in the Online Supplement, we also find that this educational positivity bias extends to popular science business books about leadership: Of the 72 leadership books on the New York Times monthly Business best-seller list from 2015 to 2026, twice as many books focused on good leadership as on bad leadership (64% vs.
This disconnect raises a broad question for leadership education, research, and practice: Are we training and selecting future leaders to best support the needs of the people working for them?
Our research suggests the current answer is No.
For organizations and institutions, the current findings are as important for selection as for training.

Investments in improved research-based selection processes that filter out the worst and most destructive leader candidates, and job termination procedures that facilitate effective removal when needed, may yield substantial positive returns for employees, organizations, and society.
Our research has several limitations, which offer directions for future work.

First, concerning Study 2, we note that employees who feel especially strongly about a bad leader may be more likely to write a review in the first place, and we do not have information about employees who chose not to review their employer, making our controlled experiments the stricter test of the "avoid-the-worst" principle.
Second, our experiments used a binary contrast between good and bad leaders.

Whether the bad-leader aversion holds when candidates are varied continuously, when good and bad qualities coexist in one candidate, or when the choice is among multiple imperfect candidates remains to be studied.
Third, Study 6's global sample coverage was constrained by the global panel provider.

Exploratory analyses found that democratic quality, corruption, and cultural power distance moderated the bad-leader aversion at the country level, but their cross-sectional nature cannot establish whether institutions causally shape the bad-leader aversion or result from it.
Future work could examine longitudinal variation within countries and natural experiments to causally test such cultural and institutional effects.
Fourth, our outcome measures focus on the willingness to sacrifice time and money.
Other forms of engagement (voice, exit, collective action, national voting) may follow different dynamics, and field studies should test whether bad-leader aversion predicts these.
Future work could also explore whether the avoid-the-worst principle extends beyond workplace supervisors to contexts such as political offices.

In our view, the current findings suggest that we are severely underestimating the value of avoiding bad leaders in organizations and society.

text.text: Glassdoor is a platform where current and former employees write structured reviews of their employers, providing separate freetext fields for positive aspects of the job (pros) and negative aspects (cons), alongside numerical ratings on overall satisfaction and several sub-dimensions, including recommending the workplace to others.
We identified leadership-relevant reviews by flagging any review in which a leadership term appeared in either the pros or cons field.
We matched manager, supervisor, and boss as bare terms, given their near-unambiguous reference to a direct leader in review text.
For less common or more ambiguous designations, we required the possessive form, my director or my team lead, to limit false positives.
Matching was case-insensitive and used word boundaries.
This procedure identified 450,343 leader-flagged reviews (4.5% of the 9,901,889 reviews in the full dataset).
We excluded firms with fewer than 10 leader-flagged reviews to ensure sufficient within-firm variation for fixed-effects estimation.
Of the 14,890 firms with at least one flagged review, this removed 10,005 firms but only 6.1% of flagged reviews (27,387 reviews).

Leader mention was coded 1 if a field contained a leader term and 0 otherwise.
